record.original_question: How can the quantum physical layer solve quantum interface problems involving information transfer and entanglement between matter qubits in nodes and photons, while also improving qubit generation rates, fidelity, and storage time enough for large-scale quantum internet deployment?

evidence.quote: the quantum physical layer is defined as the one that furnishes the quantum internet with diverse quantum assets, encompassing entanglement generation within a single hop, emission of single photons, quantum memory, interfaces between quantum light and matter, and conversion of quantum frequencies.

1. Quantum Interface Problems: These include problems such as information transfer and entanglement between matter qubits on nodes and photons as depicted in [244] [245] [246] [247] [248] [249] [250] [251] [252] [253] [254].

The quantum devices available currently are not sophisticated enough to generate qubits with very high generation rate and to maintain their quantum properties long enough [255] [256] [257] [258] [259] [260] [261] [262] [263] [264] [265] [266]. The present fidelity and storage time of the qubits need significant improvement in order for the system to be made large-scale deployment worthy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum network composed of spatially separated nodes, each containing matter qubits used for processing and storage, connected by optical channels that carry photonic qubits. The "quantum physical layer" of such a network is responsible for: (i) generating entanglement between adjacent nodes within a single hop, (ii) emitting single photons on demand, (iii) storing quantum states in quantum memories, (iv) implementing coherent interfaces between matter qubits and photonic qubits (so that quantum information can be transferred faithfully from a stationary qubit to a flying qubit and back), and (v) performing quantum frequency conversion between the wavelengths preferred by matter qubits and the telecom band suitable for low-loss fiber transmission.

Formulate and resolve the following problem:

(a) Design a physical-layer architecture (specifying the matter-qubit platform, the photon-emission mechanism, the quantum-memory protocol, the light–matter interface, and the frequency-conversion stage) that achieves deterministic, high-fidelity transfer of quantum information and on-demand entanglement generation between matter qubits at separated nodes and photons propagating between them.

(b) Within this architecture, give explicit quantitative thresholds for the qubit generation rate R, the operation/state fidelity F, and the quantum-memory storage time T, and demonstrate that these thresholds are simultaneously achievable with present or near-term devices, at levels sufficient to support large-scale (continental or global) quantum internet deployment with end-to-end entanglement distribution rates and fidelities adequate for useful applications such as device-independent quantum key distribution and distributed quantum computing.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent reviews and roadmaps on quantum networking (2024–2026) consistently identify matter–photon interfacing, quantum memory storage time, qubit generation rate, and fidelity as the principal unresolved physical-layer bottlenecks for large-scale quantum internet deployment. Demonstrations have shown progress on individual components (e.g., NV centers, trapped ions, neutral atoms, rare-earth-doped crystals), but no integrated platform has simultaneously met deployment-grade thresholds, so the problem is regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: The Quantum Internet: A Hardware Review (review article)
status_evidence.snippet: Light–matter interfaces, quantum memories, and frequency conversion remain key challenges; current devices fall short of joint thresholds for scalable deployment.
status_evidence.claim: Independent reviews corroborate that the integrated physical-layer problem remains unsolved.
